# **Software development effort estimation using COCOMO-II model with ** **FA and CFAEE**

**Sarika Mustyala** **[1]** **· Manjubala Bisi** **[1]**

Received: 31 March 2025 / Accepted: 5 November 2025
© The Author(s) under exclusive licence to The Society for Reliability Engineering, Quality and Operations Management (SREQOM), India and The
Division of Operation and Maintenance, Lulea University of Technology, Sweden 2025


**Abstract**
Software effort estimation is a critical and vital step in the
software development life cycle. Software effort estimation
has attracted significant attention from both the software
industry and the research community. Effort estimates are
crucial for determining development time, resource plan-­
ning, and budgeting. Therefore, accurately estimating effort
is essential for effective project management. Numerous
researchers have previously presented a variety of tech-­
niques for estimating software effort, including statistical,
algorithmic, machine learning-based, and nature-inspired
models. Selecting the most accurate estimation method is
a complex procedure. This study optimizes the COCOMOII model parameters for estimation accuracy by employing
the Firefly Algorithm(FA) and the Chaotic Firefly Algo-­
rithm with Enhanced Exploration (CFAEE). Mean Mag-­
nitude of Relative Error (MMRE) and Prediction (PRED)
are used to assess the application of the two models on six
datasets. While the Firefly Algorithm surpasses previous
algorithms, the results show that the CFAEE methodology
is the most effective approach for determining the effi-­
ciency coefficients of the COCOMO-II model. Statistical
testing also shows that the proposed model yields better
results.

**Keywords** COCOMO-II model · Effort estimation ·
Parameters optimization · Firefly algorithm · Chaotic
firefly algorithm with enhanced exploration

Sarika Mustyala

manjubalabisi@nitw.ac.in

**1 Introduction**

The number of software projects that exceed their budget
and take longer than expected to finish is one of the main
problems software project managers encounter. Inaccurate
estimates have frequently led to projects being over bud-­
get, behind schedule, and ultimately abandoned. Despite
exceeding budget or time, thirty to forty percent of software
projects were eventually completed, and numerous addi-­
tional projects were scrapped or failed (Nisar et al. 2008).
Besides various causes of failure, a significant portion of
software development failures have been traced back to
inaccurate software estimations (Papic 2019; Attarzadeh
and Ow 2011). There are several issues with software effort
prediction when developing software projects. In develop-­
ing a software project, estimating effort and costs is criti-­
cal. Effort and cost estimation involves predicting the work
and resources required to complete project tasks, typically
measured in labor hours and financial expenses. It is help-­
ful when offering services to meet clients’ functional needs
(Fernández-Diego et al. 2020). There are numerous rea-­
sons why software projects run behind schedule, including
unpredictable and unreliable production that is hard for soft-­
ware project managers to manage. Communication issues
can also cause delays and failures in software projects, mak-­
ing it complex to forecast the development effort for these
projects.

Boehm stated that 20% of the project duration and 8% of
all resources are allocated to developing baseline require-­
ments. Most software projects effectively utilize between
7% and 15% of the project’s overall resources. The project
attribute under consideration explains the features of the
link to a software engineering project (Putri et al. 2021).
The Constructive Cost Model (COCOMO) II is a widely
used strategy in the software industry for estimating soft-­
ware efforts. Numerous enhancements in various cost driv-­
ers have demonstrated their increased accuracy (Putri et al.
## 1 3

2021). Organizations’ methods and processes for determin-­
ing estimates for project planning, probability estimates,
and proposal bidding are collectively referred to as software
effort estimation (Agarwal et al. 2001; Jorgensen 2005). As
a result, managers, professionals who perform or rely on
effort estimating, technical personnel, and executives have
severe concerns about estimation accuracy (Kemerer 1987;
Jain et al. 2024; Mustyala and Bisi 2025). The need for
more reliable estimates makes it challenging for software
engineering researchers to estimate software development
efforts accurately (Kaushik et al. 2022).

Software effort estimation models are categorized into
two main approaches: algorithmic and non-algorithmic. The
Constructive Cost Model (COCOMO) (Boehm 1984) and
Software Life Cycle Management (SLIM) (Putnam 1978)
are examples of algorithmic models, developed through
statistical analysis of historical data (Manchala and Bisi
2024). Well-known algorithmic effort estimation models
include Putnam’s SLIM (Putnam 1978), Function Point
Analysis (Boehm et al. 2000), and Boehm’s COCOMO-I
and II (Boehm et al. 2000). However, obtaining the inputs
that these models require early in the software development
process, such as the number of user screens, interfaces,
source lines of code (SLOC), and complexity, can be timeconsuming and effort-intensive. Despite this, these models
are relatively simple to understand, and their formulas and
calculations provide quick estimates compared to non-algo-­
rithmic models.

Among the wide variety of estimating models, algo-­
rithmic constructs like the Constructive Cost Model

(COCOMO) and its descendants, COCOMO-II, remain
popular due to their ease of use and adaptability to vari-­
ous project phases (Boehm 1984; Boehm et al. 1995). The
input parameters plays a crucial role in these models’ accu-­
racy, and this dependence can lead to substantial estimation
mistakes. Machine learning approaches and metaheuristic
algorithms have improved estimation accuracy by refining
parameter values, making these models more reliable (Mah-­
mood et al. 2022).

Metaheuristic algorithms have been recommended for
their ability to quickly find near-optimal solutions, which
makes them ideal for handling complex optimization prob-­
lems in software effort estimation. For estimating pur-­
poses, a meta-heuristic method is currently used to improve
forecast results and yield accurate outcomes (Putri et al.
2021). When compared to other optimization techniques,
COCOMO-II’s effort estimation calculation needs to be
more accurate| (Chalotra et al. 2015; Jafari and Ziaaddini
2016; Hidayat et al. 2016). To increase the accuracy of effort
in software projects, this study combines COCOMO-II and
the Firefly algorithm(FA) and Chaotic FA with Enhanced
## 1 3


International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

Exploration (CFAEE) to optimize COCOMO-II model
coefficients (A,B) values.

We have applied the FA and CFAEE models to the six
datasets, NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81, China, Deshar-­
nais, and Maxwell. The actual effort of the projects in the
dataset is expressed in Person-Months and hours. The results
show that the proposed CFAEE effectively optimizes the
COCOMO-II model’s coefficients (A and B), as evidenced
by improved MMRE and PRED evaluation metrics. In par-­
ticular, we will focus on the following research questions:

RQ1: How do the coefficient values for COCOMO-II,
obtained from CFAEE, demonstrate a better understanding
or representation of the complexities involved in software
projects compared to conventional methods?

RQ2: What is the potential impact on effort estima-­
tion accuracy in the COCOMO-II model of integrating
the Chaotic Firefly Algorithm with Enhanced Exploration
(CFAEE)?

The paper’s organization is as follows: The relevant
work on effort estimation is presented in Sect. 2, and the
background work is presented in Sect. 3. Section 4 presents
the methodology. The achieved outcomes are presented in
Sect. 5, following the discussion. Section 6 discusses our
experimental study’s validity threats. Finally, a conclusion
is included in Sect. 7 of the study.

**2 Related work**

Software development effort estimation is a crucial compo-­
nent of project management. An overestimation or under-­
estimation of it has a negative impact on the project’s
resources. It is important to note that research has used
many metaheuristic algorithms to enhance the COCOMOII model’s performance. To improve the COCOMO-II
model’s estimation accuracy, Fadhil et al. (2020) applied
the dolphin algorithm and introduced the DolBat, a hybrid
approach that combines the bat and dolphin algorithms. The
MMRE metric evaluated the models tested on the NASA93

and NASA60 datasets. The Bat algorithm, the Genetic
algorithm, the hybrid Cuckoo Optimization and Harmony
Search algorithm (CSHS), and the original COCOMO-II
model were compared with their (Fadhil et al. 2020) sug-­
gested model.

Applying the Self-Organizing Migrating Algorithm
(SOMA), Bajusova et al. (2024) suggested improving
software effort estimation in their study. Compared to con-­
ventional techniques like COCOMO, they attained better
estimation accuracy by integrating SOMA. Their findings
demonstrated better PRED values and notable decreases
in MMRE. They emphasized on how evolutionary algo-­
rithms can solve challenging optimization issues in software

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

project management. Parwita et al. (2017) also sought to
optimize the coefficients of the COCOMO-II model using
the Cuckoo Optimization Algorithm (COA). They car-­
ried out their analysis on the Turkish Software Dataset
and made comparisons between the Fuzzy Local Calibra-­
tion Model and the initial COCOMO-II model. Attarzadeh

and Ow (2011) suggested employing an adaptive fuzzy
logic approach to increase COCOMO-II estimation accu-­
racy. This method improved effort prediction accuracy by
adapting dynamically to project-specific characteristics.
Compared to standard COCOMO-II, the results showed a
considerable improvement in MMRE and PRED metrics.
The study emphasized how fuzzy logic may improve soft-­
ware effort estimating models.

Langsari and Sarno optimized the COCOMO-II model
(Langsari and Sarno 2017) using the Turkish Software Data-­
set, with an emphasis on the Particle Swarm Optimization
(PSO) algorithm, which proved to be superior to both the
Tabu Search algorithm and the initial COCOMO-II coeffi-­
cients. Jafari and Ziaaddini (2016) used the harmony search
method to optimize software cost estimation. Compared to
conventional approaches, their methodology significantly
improved MMRE & PRED metrics by adjusting estimat-­
ing parameters to increase accuracy. The paper emphasized
harmony search’s usefulness in software engineering and
shows how the algorithm can be used to improve effort
estimating models. Hidayat et al. (2016) offered a pattern
reduction enhanced by using an ant colony optimization
clustering technique to increase clustering efficiency. Their
method preserved the clustering quality while lowering
computational complexity by including pattern reduction.
The technique’s significance in data mining & pattern rec-­
ognition techniques was highlighted by the study, which
demonstrates notable performance advantages and efficacy
in handling big datasets.

To enhance the effectiveness of the fundamental
COCOMO model, Gandomani et al. (2022) employed a
hybrid GA-EA strategy, which combines a genetic algo-­
rithm (GA) with environmental adaptation (EA) techniques.
The incorporation of EA successfully resolved the conver-­
gence problem with GA. The EA method, the hybrid model
GA-EA, and the primary COCOMO model were used in a
comparative study. According to the data, the hybrid GA-EA
strategy produced the best outcomes. The effectiveness of
the Gray Wolf Algorithm (GWO), Harmony Search Algo-­
rithm (HSA), and Strawberry Algorithm (SBA) was inves-­
tigated by Hassan and Khan (2021). These optimization
methods were used with the NASA93 dataset and a 3-fold

cross-validation strategy on the fundamental COCOMO
model. The study took into account both embedded and


semidetached types as well as the entire dataset. The study
aimed to lower MMRE, and its outcomes indicated that
GWO outperformed the other algorithms.

Fatima Ezzahra Boujida et al. systematically review neu-­
ral networks for software development effort estimation,
highlighting their ability to model complex relationships
and outperform traditional methods. It identified challenges
like dataset quality and overfitting while emphasizing future
directions, including hybrid models and explainable AI
(Boujida et al. 2024). Kumari and Pushkar put forth a unique
model for modifying the fundamental COCOMO model
parameters (Kumari and Pushkar 2015), based on the meta-­
heuristic Cuckoo Search algorithm. This model was tested
using the NASA93 dataset with MMRE as the fitness func-­
tion. Bacanin et al. (2021) presented a new Chaotic Firefly
Algorithm (CFA) to improve global optimization problem
exploration capabilities. Chaotic map integration enhances
the algorithm’s ability to escape local optima and find global
solutions. The authors employed dropout regularization to
demonstrate the effectiveness of the CFA, showing its supe-­
rior performance compared to conventional techniques.

Yang explained the Firefly Algorithm (FA), a unique
optimization method inspired by fireflies’ flashing habits
(Yang 2009). The Firefly Algorithm (FA) effectively han-­
dles multi-modal optimization by balancing exploration and
exploitation, outperforming conventional methods in find-­
ing global optima. Yang’s foundational work had led to the
widespread adoption of FA. To enhance its performance,
Wang et al. (2017) introduced an adaptive FA that dynami-­
cally adjusts control parameters during the search, resulting
in faster convergence and improved solution accuracy. This
highlights ongoing efforts to refine nature-inspired optimi-­
zation techniques.

A Chaotic Gravitational Search Algorithm (CGSA) was
used by Li et al. (2012) introduced a method for identifying
parameters in chaotic systems. The technique uses chaotic
sequences to prevent premature convergence and improve
exploration during gravitational search. Compared to con-­
ventional approaches, their results showed better robustness
and accuracy in recognizing chaotic system parameters.
The importance of optimizing algorithmic parameters for
enhancing predictive performance across a range of soft-­
ware engineering activities has been highlighted by recent
studies. Accurate hyperparameter tuning greatly improves
the prediction models’ accuracy (Brown et al. 2023). In this
work, we have employed CFAEE, which uses adaptive and
chaotic exploration processes to calibrate the COCOMO-II
parameters (A and B) as optimally as possible and to pro-­
vide consistent results across diverse data sets.

**3 Background**

**3.1 Constructive cost model II**

Barry W. Boehm created a model called the COnstructive
COst MOdel (COCOMO), which consists of 63 differ-­
ent sample projects. Boehm proposed three categories of
COCOMO modes. According to Boehm (1984), the three
modes are: basic, intermediate, and detailed. The effort is
estimated using different input parameters based on the
model type. These features include the number of lines
of code (KLOC) for the project, 15 cost driver attributes,
and the calibration constants (A, B, C, and D), whose val-­
ues vary depending on whether the project is embedded,
semi-detached, or organic. The values of these calibra-­
tion constants are specified in Table 1, which is the project
description.

Based on the project size and calibration constants (A,
B), the fundamental COCOMO model (Eq. 1) computes
effort expressed in person-months (PM) (Boehm 1984).
The effort required to develop the software does not grow
linearly with the project’s size, as exponent (B) indicates.
With Eq. 2, where C and D are calibration constants, one
can find the time necessary for software development *T* Dev
in calendar months.

Effort[PM] = *A ·* (KLOC) *[B]*  (1)


International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

T Dev = *C ·* (Effort) *[D]*  (2)

The intermediate model estimates the software development
effort in terms of man-months by considering the size of the
code, which is measured in thousands of lines. It adjusts the
estimated value using the empirical constants A and B. Proj-­
ect attributes are defined through 15 drivers, each associated
with a specific numerical value known as a multiplier. The
estimated effort for COCOMO-II is calculated using Eq. 3.


where Size is expressed in kilo lines of code (KLOC) and

Model multipliers stand for the following factors: computer,
product, personnel, and project factors. Driver multiplier
values have been assigned based on the following six cat-­
egories: Very Low, Low, Nominal, High, Very High, and
Extra High. Table 2 provides the precise values (Boehm
1984).

Several improvements were made by the COCOMOII paradigm, including reuse, object-oriented methodol-­
ogy, and non-sequential development (Boehm et al. 1995).
This model defines three submodels: the Post-Architecture
model, the Early Design model, and the Applications com-­
position model.

Application composition model is applied when compo-­
nent-based development or prototyping is done in the soft-­
ware development’s early stages (Boehm et al. 2000). To
estimate the effort, count the object points, correct for reus-­
ability, and then multiply the result by productivity rates.
When a detailed system design is unavailable in the early
stages of development, the Early Design model is employed

to determine a preliminary estimate (Boehm et al. 2000).
This model uses thousands of lines of code or raw function

points to represent the software size, along with a set of 7
effort multipliers and five scaling factors. Conversion tables
can translate function pointers into source code (LOC) lines.
Compared to the Early Design Model, the Post-Architecture
model offers more precise estimates because it is based on
detailed system specifications and can be used in the devel-­
opment or maintenance phase (Bajusova et al. 2024).

**3.2 Firefly algorithm and FA with explicit**
**exploration mechanism**

The Firefly Algorithm (FA) is based on fireflies’ social
and flashing properties. The FA mimics the natural system
using several approximation principles because it is highly
sophisticated and complicated in the“real world” (Yang
2009; Khoshniat et al. 2024). Fitness functions are repre-­
sented as firefly attractiveness and brightness; in most FA
implementations, attractiveness depends on brightness,
which is determined by the value of the objective function.
When handling minimization problems, it is represented as
follows:


Each firefly employs attraction *β*, which is directly related
to the luminous intensity of a specific firefly and depends on
distance, as shown by Eq. 7.

where attractiveness is indicated at distance r = 0 by param-­
eter *β* 0 . Note that, in reality, Eq. 8 is frequently used in place
of Eq. 7 (Yang 2009).

The Chaotic Firefly Algorithm with Enhanced Explora-­
tion (CFAEE) is an advanced optimization technique that
outperforms the traditional Firefly Algorithm. The algo-­
rithm initiates a population of fireflies, evaluates their fit-­
ness using a predetermined objective function, and then
updates the fireflies based on their decreasing attractiveness
with distance, determined by a light absorption coefficient.
To prevent premature convergence and escape local optima,
## 1 3


International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

the algorithm uses chaotic maps to dynamically adjust the
randomization parameter, thereby enhancing each firefly’s
migration towards brighter ones (i.e., those with superior fit-­
ness). Crucially, boundary management ensures that every
firefly remains within the allowed search spaces, thereby
maintaining the algorithm’s efficiency. The algorithm
updates the firefly positions and fitness, ultimately yielding
an optimal or nearly ideal solution. The optimal solution
is refined over successive generations until the maximum
number of repetitions is reached. The pseudo code for
CFAEE is as follows:

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

A detailed explanation of CFAEE is as follows:
Explicit exploration aids in exploring the parameter
boundaries for the current optimal individual *y* *[∗]* at late
execution phases. At the same time, in early iterations, it
aims to ensure the algorithm eventually reaches the optimal
portion of the search area. Each solution is modeled using
an additional characteristics trial to integrate this behavior;
this trial is incremented each time the basic FA search fails

to enhance the solution using Eq. 9. The random solution
chosen from within the search space is substituted for the
individual when the trial parameter for that solution hits a
predefined limit value using the same process as in the setup
phase:

*y* *i,j* = *L* *j* + ( *U* *j* *−* *L* *j* ) *·* Rand  (12)

where *y* *i,j* denotes the j-th component of the i-th individual,
*U* *j* and *L* *j* represent upper and lower search boundaries of
the j-th element, and the Rand is a random number with a
uniform distribution from the interval [0, 1].

When the algorithm fails to explore the appropriate por-­
tions of the search region during the early iterations, replac-­
ing the exhausted solution with a pseudo-random individual
disrupts search performance. However, this replacement
consumes function evaluations in later iterations, assuming
the best region has already been identified.

*y* *i,j* = *PL* *j* + ( *PU* *j* *−* *PL* *j* ) *·* Rand  (13)

where the lowest and greatest values of the j-th component
for the total population P are denoted by *PL* *j* and *PU* *j*,
respectively.

In deterministic and nonlinear systems, chaos is a random
phenomenon susceptible to its beginning circumstances
(Alatas 2010; Santos Coelho and Mariani 2008). The sug-­
gested approach uses a logistic map (Li et al. 2012) that is
defined as follows and is executed in K steps.

*σ* *i,j* *[k]* [+1] = *µσ* *i,j* *[k]* [(1] *[ −]* *[σ]* *[i,j]* [)] *[,]* *k* = 1 *,* 2 *, . . ., K*  (14)

where *µ* is the control variable and *σ* *i,j* *[k]* [ and ] *[σ]* *i,j* *[k]* [+1] [ repre-­]
sent the chaotic variables for the *j* -th element of the *i* -th
solution in steps *k* and *k* + 1, respectively. As this value
has already been determined empirically (Mirjalili 2016),
*σ* *i,j* *̸* = 0 *.* 25 *,* 0 *.* 5 *,* and0 *.* 75, *σ* *i,j* *∈* (0 *,* 1), and *µ* are set to 4.

At every phase *k*, new *y* *[∗]*, sometimes called *y* *[∗]* *[′]*, is gener-­
ated by applying Eqs. 15 and 16 to component *j* of *y* *[∗]* :

*y* *j* *[∗]* *[′]* [= (1] *[ −]* *[L]* [)] *[ ·][ y]* *j* *[∗]* [+] *[ l][ ·][ S]* *[j]* [ ] (15)

*S* *j* = *L* *j* + *σ* *j* *[k]* *[·]* [ (] *[U]* *[j]* *[−]* *[L]* *[j]* [)]  (16)


*λ* = [mffe] *[ −]* [ffe][ + 1]  (17)

ffe

where *λ* is the dynamic shrinkage parameter that is depen-­
dent on the maximum number of fitness function evalu-­
ations (mffe) in the process, as well as the current fitness
function evaluation (ffe). Dynamic *λ* improves the exploi-­
tation-exploration stability around the *⃗y* *[∗]* . The implementa-­
tion is done in phases, with a more targeted exploitation in
the latter stages and a more extensive search radius within
*⃗y* *[∗]* being examined in the earlier stages.

**4 Methodology**

**4.1 Problem representation**

Accurate software effort estimation is essential for efficient
project management and resource allocation. The intricate
and nonlinear relationships between project features and
development effort pose a problem for standard models
such as the COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model) regard-­
ing parameter optimization (Bajusova et al. 2024). Since the
model is static, it is less successful at adjusting to contempo-­
rary software projects’ complex and dynamic settings. This
unpredictability frequently leads to inconsistent estimations.

Because of this, parametric models such as COCOMO
frequently generate estimates that are inconsistent and less
accurate, particularly when applied in situations that are
significantly different from those in which the models were
initially calibrated. Moreover, these models’ parameter tun-­
ing procedures are usually manual or dependent on histori-­
cal data, which makes it challenging to adjust to changing
organizational settings, development methodologies, or
technology.

These challenges underscore a critical research need for
adaptive and flexible optimization techniques capable of
dynamically adjusting the parameters of estimation models
to better reflect real-world software development scenarios.
Consequently, there is a need to create and assess improved
optimization techniques to improve the accuracy of effort
estimating models. Among existing approaches, the Firefly
Algorithm (FA) has demonstrated promise in optimization
tasks across benchmark problems and real-world applica-­
tions (Yang and He 2013). However, the basic FA suffers
from several limitations, including premature convergence,
weak intensification, and poor balance between exploration
and exploitation (Strumberger et al. 2017). These issues are
particularly problematic in the early stages of search, where
a lack of diversity can prevent the algorithm from locating
optimal regions in the solution space.
## 1 3

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management


**Fig. 1** Flowchart for development
effort estimation using COCOMO-II
optimized by CFAEE
## 1 3

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

To overcome these limitations, this study investigates the
use of the Chaotic Firefly Algorithm with Explicit Explora-­
tion (CFAEE), which enhances the original FA by integrat-­
ing chaotic dynamics and a targeted exploration strategy.
This enables more robust parameter optimization in effort
estimation models, resulting in enhanced adaptability,
increased accuracy, and more reliable support for software
project planning.

**4.2 Proposed approach COCOMO-II with CFAEE**

The chaotic Firefly algorithm with enhanced exploration
(CFAEE) has been used in this study to optimize the coef-­
ficient values of the COCOMO-II model and forecast soft-­
1
ware effort in the initial phase. Figure shows the flowchart
of the proposed approach. This approach shows the ability
of CFAEE to explore complex search spaces effectively
with the integration of CFAEE and COCOMO-II to improve
exploration and avoid local optima. This integration also
aims to enhance the accuracy of the model’s prediction by
optimizing parameters through a metaheuristic approach
inspired by the natural behavior of fireflies.

In software effort estimation, the challenge faced by the
COCOMO-II model is the significant nonlinear relation-­
ship between inputs and predicted effort. Small changes can
have a significant impact on output; hence, the parameter
tuning procedure must traverse a delicate and complicated
search space. This results in a landscape with noise, sparse
data, and several local optima. Exploring methods that can
better manage the balance between global exploration and
local exploitation in such complex areas is still necessary,
even though a variety of metaheuristics, including Genetic
methods, Particle Swarm Optimization, and others, have
been used in this field. FA and CFAEE effectively handle
the nonlinear and complex nature of software effort estima-­
tion and adapt well across diverse datasets without requiring


structural modifications. They rely solely on objective func-­
tions such as MMRE and PRED, making them suitable
for data-driven, black-box optimization and robust against
noisy or incomplete input conditions common in early proj-­
ect phases. Our research particularly examines whether the
Firefly Algorithm and its chaotic-enhanced variant are more
suitable for handling the estimated problems presented by
this field of study.

We chose FA and CFAEE for the following reasons. In
complicated problem domains like software effort estimat-­
ing, the (FA) and its improved variant, the (CFAEE), are
preferred over several other algorithms because of their
potent ability to strike a balance between exploration and
exploitation (Yang 2009). Inspired by the behavior of fire-­
flies, FA excels at finding optimal solutions while avoiding
local optima, which makes it helpful in managing the multidimensional and non-linear nature of software projects. By
adding chaotic maps to FA, CFAEE improves its capabili-­
ties even further. By preventing premature convergence and
promoting better exploration, these maps help the algorithm
better negotiate the complex linkages in software projects.
Studies comparing methods demonstrate that CFAEE per-­
forms better in accuracy than GA and Bat Algorithm, with
much lower MMRE and higher PRED(25) values, demon-­
strating its superiority in generating more dependable effort
estimates.

Many crucial phases are involved in integrating
COCOMO-II with CFAEE to increase effort estimation
accuracy. The main goal of this integration is to use CFAEE,
a metaheuristic approach of optimization inspired by firefly
behavior with chaotic mapping, to optimize the COCOMOII model’s estimation parameters to improve explora-­
tion capabilities. Iterative evaluations and refinements are
involved in this integration process to ensure the optimized
parameters produce reliable effort estimates across different
datasets.
## 1 3

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management


**Algorithm 1** Algorithm for CFAEE with COCOMO-II Model
## 1 3

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

An enhanced metaheuristic optimization technique called
the Chaotic Firefly Algorithm with Enhanced Exploration
(CFAEE)is used to improve software effort estimation using
the COCOMO-II model. This method addresses the diffi-­
culties and uncertainties involved in software development.
Also, this method combines increased exploration mecha-­
nisms, chaotic dynamics, and the concepts of the firefly
algorithm, as shown in Algorithm 1.

The CFAEE algorithm begins by initializing several vital
parameters to define the search space and control the optimi-­
zation process. The number of fireflies (possible solutions)
and the maximal amount of iterations are metaheuristic con-­
trol parameters *n* and *NT* . The problem’s dimensionality,
*D*, is represented by the search space parameters *l* *j* and *u* *j*,
which denote the bottom and upper bounds of each dimen-­
sion. The light absorption coefficient, *γ*, the initial attrac-­
tiveness coefficient, *β* 0, the initial randomization parameter,
*α* 0, the minimum randomization parameter, *K*, the number
of local search iterations, and *ϕ*, a parameter governing
the exploration strategy are some of the specific CFAEE
parameters.

The procedure produces an initial population of fireflies.
It is represented as *P* init = *{y* *i,j* *}*, where *i* is the firefly index
and *j* is the parameter index. Equation 12 uses a random ini-­
tialization function to randomly initialize each firefly’s posi-­
tion inside the specified constraints. A proposed solution
with parameters for the COCOMO-II model is represented
by each firefly *y* *i* = ( *A, B* ) . The Mean Magnitude of Rela-­
tive Error (MMRE) and Prediction at level 0.25 (PRED),
which are computed by Eqs. 19 and 20, respectively, are
used to evaluate the initial fitness of each solution.

The algorithm uses the COCOMO-II model to assess
each firefly solution’s fitness during each iteration of the
optimization process. The fireflies are compared, and those
with better fitness (lower MMRE or higher PRED) attract
other fireflies. Equation 9 computes the attractiveness of a
solution, and Eq. 7 updates the solution dynamically with
distance to ascertain the direction of firefly movement. This
process ensures that less fit fireflies are pulled towards more
optimal regions of the search space.

To prevent early convergence and preserve diversity,
CFAEE utilizes explicit exploration techniques. Each firefly
is associated with a trial parameter that tracks the number


of rounds without improvement. Equation 12 controls the
replacement of a firefly’s trial with a new random solution
inside the search space when its trial exceeds a predeter-­
mined limit. A state of equilibrium is avoided, and this
random replacement promotes population diversity. As the
algorithm develops, a guided replacement method becomes
increasingly essential. This technique concentrates the
search on the most likely solutions *y* *[∗]* by utilizing parameter
values from the current population. This guided technique
(Eq. 13) generates new solutions that increase the effective-­
ness of the search.

The gBest Chaotic Local Search (CLS) technique is used
to refine results further. Equation 14 introduces chaotic
dynamics, which produce chaotic sequences that perturb the
best solution *y* *[∗]* at now and lead to other candidate solu-­
tions *y* *[′∗]* (Eq. 16). Based on shrinkage parameters and per-­
formance improvements, the algorithm determines whether
to replace or keep the original solution (Eq. 17). This guar-­
antees weaker solutions are replaced or improved through
focused search and chaotic perturbations.

As the algorithm nears its final stages, it identifies the
optimal parameters for the COCOMO-II model by mini-­
mizing MMRE and maximizing PRED. Modifying the
COCOMO-II model with the optimal parameters improves
the model’s predictive accuracy for software effort estima-­
tion. Software developers benefit from this refinement as
it produces more accurate effort estimates that help with
resource allocation and project planning.

By integrating guided replacement techniques, chaotic
dynamics, and explicit exploration, CFAEE offers a robust
basis for COCOMO-II model parameter optimization. This
methodology guarantees efficient exploration throughout
the solution domain and enhances the model’s precision in
predicting software development endeavors. The datasets
NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, and
Maxwell validate the algorithm’s performance and demon-­
strate the algorithm’s ability to improve software effort esti-­
mation and facilitate improved decision-making in software
project management.

To illustrate the optimization mechanism of the proposed
CFAEE algorithm, consider a project from the NASA93
dataset with a size of 16 KLOC and an actual effort of 114
person-months. Using the standard COCOMO-II model

with the default parameters *A* = 2 *.* 94 and *B* = 0 *.* 91,
the estimated effort obtained from Eq. 3 is 46.79 personmonths. To improve this prediction, the CFAEE algorithm
steps to be applied as follows:

Initially, a random population of fireflies is generated
within the predefined bounds for the parameters *A* and
*B* ( *l* *j* *≤* *y* *i,j* *≤* *u* *j* ) according to the initialization rule in
Eq. 12.

- Each firefly *y* *i* = ( *A, B* ) represents a candidate solution
whose brightness (fitness) is computed using the CO-­
COMO-II estimation model defined in Eq. 3 and evalu-­
ated through the MMRE criterion.

- During each iteration ( *t < N* *T* ), the fireflies move to-­
ward brighter ones using the attractiveness function in
Eq. 9, where the attractiveness decreases with distance
as defined by Eq. 7.

For example, in the initial iteration, a promising can-­
didate with parameters ( *A* = 3 *.* 10 *, B* = 0 *.* 94) yields an
estimated effort of 56.76 person-months. As the itera-­
tions progress, the chaotic factor *λ* and dynamic control
## 1 3


parameter *α* are updated through Eqs. 11 and 17 to balance
exploration and exploitation, enabling the algorithm to
refine parameter values such as ( *A* = 2 *.* 98 *, B* = 0 *.* 99)
and ( *A* = 3 *.* 00 *, B* = 1 *.* 01), which produce estimated
efforts of 59.82 and 62.59 person-months, respectively.

- When the iteration count reaches the threshold *ϕ*, ran-­
dom and guided replacements are performed using
Eqs. 12 and 13 to maintain diversity, followed by the
gBest-based Chaotic Local Search (CLS) strategy de-­
fined in Eqs. 14–16 to further exploit the best solution.

After the maximum number of iterations, the algorithm con-­
verges with optimized parameters *A* = 3 *.* 00 and *B* = 1 *.* 01 .
The final estimated effort of 62.59 person-months, obtained
from Eq. 3 using these optimized values, is significantly
closer to the actual effort than the default COCOMO-II esti-­
mate of 46.79 person-months, demonstrating how CFAEE
systematically improves parameter accuracy and directs the
search toward more reliable effort predictions.

**5 Result analysis**

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis, comparing
the performance of the COCOMO-II model with the Cha-­
otic Firefly Algorithm with Enhanced Exploration (CFAEE)
against several well-known models. These include the
COCOMO-II model, the CSHS model, the Genetic Algo-­
rithm (GA) model, the Bat algorithm, the Dolphin algo-­
rithm, the Dolphin Bat algorithm, and the basic Firefly
algorithm. The comparison is conducted using two robust
evaluation measures, the Mean Magnitude of Relative Error
(MMRE) and Prediction at level X=0.25 (PRED(X)), on the
NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, and

Maxwell datasets.

**5.1 Datasets**

The NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81, China, Desharnais,
and Maxwell datasets were used in this study as the primary


sources of empirical data to assess how well software effort
estimating models performed. Because they contain exten-­
sive real-world project data, these datasets are well-recog-­
nized and perfect for benchmarking and verifying estimating
methodologies. COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, Maxwell
datasets (Jones 2020), and NASA’s software development
projects compile the NASA93 and NASA60 (Fadhil et al.
2020) datasets. The datasets used in this study are prepro-­
cessed and obtained directly from the (Jones 2020). The
description of the datasets used is shown in Table 3.

**5.2 Evaluation metrics**

MMRE (Mean Magnitude of Relative Error) and
PRED(0.25) are the metrics used to assess the predictive
models’ accuracy. The Magnitude of Relative Error (MRE)
represents the relative error of an individual prediction by
expressing the absolute difference between the estimated
and actual effort as a proportion of the actual effort. The

Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE) measures the
average relative difference between estimated and actual
effort needed for a software project. It is computed by divid-­
ing the absolute error by the actual effort for each project
and averaging the results. A lower MMRE indicates better
estimation accuracy, reflecting smaller average deviations
from actual effort values (Mensah et al. 2018; Mustyala
et al. 2025; Singal et al. 2022). The equations for Magnitude
of Relative Error(MRE) and MMRE are given in the Eqs.
18 and 19.

**5.3 Base models**

To illustrate the advantage of the proposed model, we have
compared it with the COCOMO-II model using a few esti-­
mating approaches: the GA model (Alajlan and Tagoug
2016), CSHS model (Puspaningrum and Sarno 2017), Bat
(Ibrahim 2016), Dolphin and Dolphin Bat (Fadhil et al.
2020). The genetic algorithm optimizes the parameters of
the COCOMO-II model to achieve more accurate estimates
of software effort and development time. By integrating
the exploration capabilities of cuckoo Search(CS) with the
fine-tuning abilities of Harmony Search(HS), the hybrid
approach aims to optimize the parameters of software effort
estimation models, leading to improved estimation accu-­
racy. The bat method is used to fine-tune the software effort
estimation model parameters by mimicking the echoloca-­
tion behavior of bats, thereby enhancing prediction accu-­
racy. Similarly, the Dolphin Bat approach optimizes the
model parameters to improve the precision of software
development effort predictions. The algorithm is useful for
software project management because the results show how
well it navigates the search area to reduce estimation errors.

Python is used to implement our proposed model,
CFAEE. Using the methodology in Sect. 4, we integrated
COCOMO-II with CFAEE and compared it with different
benchmarking models used in Fadhil et al. (2020). This
comparison shows the advantages of our proposed model,
COCOMO-II and CFAEE, in software effort estimation
optimization and highlights its possibilities to improve the
accuracy of software project management.

**5.4 Results of effort estimation**

From each of the six datasets, NASA93, NASA60,
COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, and Maxwell, we have
chosen a subset of projects to ensure variation in project
features and estimation scenarios. Tables 4 to 9 present the
results of the estimation for these projects. These tables


where, *E* *i* is the actual effort, *E* [ˆ] *i* is the predicted effort, the
number of projects is represented by f, the total number of
projects with an MRE value of below or equivalent to 0.25
is represented by parameter ’A’.

PRED(0.25) Fadhil et al. (2020), another name for Pre-­
diction at the 25% threshold, assesses the percentage of
projects whose anticipated effort is within a given range
of the actual effort. It gauges the proportion of projects,
namely, when the expected effort and actual effort are within
25% of each other. Calculating the proportion of forecasts
that closely match the exact values aids in evaluating how
effectively the model predicts effort. When a model’s pre-­
dictions are closer to the actual effort, as seen by a greater
PRED(0.25) score, it is constructive in real-world situa-­
tions where estimates must fall within a specific range to be
deemed trustworthy (Mensah et al. 2018). The equation for
PRED is shown in Eq. 20.

compare the effort estimation for each project using the
COCOMO-II model integrated with CFAEE against various
benchmarking models like Genetic Algorithm(GA), CSHS,
Bat, Dolphin Bat, and the Firefly Algorithm. It is evident
that the CFAEE model consistently performs well in esti-­
mating project efforts, often outperforming the other bench-­
marking models.

Table 4 represents the effort estimation results for ten
projects chosen from the NASA93 dataset. These findings
show that the CFAEE model’s effort estimations are gener-­
ally within a reasonable range of the actual efforts in various
projects. For example, the CFAEE model predicts the effort
for Project 1 at 69.98 person-months, which is extremely
close to the 117.6 person-months that the actual effort is.
This closeness between estimated and actual efforts is a
recurrent pattern in the chosen projects, suggesting that the
optimization strategies of the CFAEE model, like increased
exploration mechanisms and chaotic dynamics, are helpful
for fine-tuning effort estimations. Compared to the other
models, including the COCOMO-II, CSHS, GA, Bat, and
Dolphin Bat algorithms, and the FA model, the CFAEE
model shows a remarkable capacity to approximate efforts.

The results of the effort estimation for the projects chosen
from the dataset NASA60 are represented in Table 5. The
CFAEE model demonstrates remarkable accuracy in esti-­
mating efforts that closely match the actual efforts for each
project. For Instance, Project 1 predicts an effort of 5.81
person-months, remarkably close to the actual effort of 8.4
person-months. This pattern is consistent across other proj-­
ects, highlighting the CFAEE model’s ability to represent
the basic nature of the effort estimates accurately. The close-­
ness between effort estimates and actual values across dif-­
ferent projects suggests that the CFAEE model’s increased
exploration mechanisms and chaotic dynamics are skilled
at fine-tuning effort estimates, resulting in more dependable
and accurate forecasts.

Table 6 represents the effort estimation results for seven
projects chosen from the COCOMO81 dataset. For exam-­
ple, the CFAEE model predicts the effort for Project 60 at
42.3099 person-months, which is extremely close to the
actual effort of 57 person-months. The selected projects
consistently exhibit this proximity between estimated and


real efforts, indicating that the CFAEE model’s optimization
techniques-such as enhanced exploration mechanisms and
chaotic dynamics-are useful for optimizing effort estimates.

The results of the effort estimation for the projects chosen
from the dataset China, Desharnais, and Maxwell are repre-­
sented in Tables 7, 8, 9.


The CFAEE model accurately estimates efforts for each
project, closely matching the actual efforts. For example, in
the China dataset, Project 100 predicts an effort of 879.8786
person-hours, which is close to the actual effort of 943 per-­
son-hours. In the Desharnais dataset, Project 70 estimates
an effort of 1100.0012, which is nearer to the actual effort of
1155 person-hours.

The actual effort of Project 50 in the Maxwell dataset is
5931 person-hours. Our model predicted 4841.9648 personhours, which is closer to the actual effort compared to the
other models, as shown in the Table 9. This trend is con-­
sistent across various projects among different datasets,
demonstrating how well the CFAEE model captures the fun-­
damentals of the effort estimates. Given how closely effort
estimates and actual values across many projects match, it is
likely that the CFAEE model’s enhanced exploration mech-­
anisms and chaotic dynamics are adept at optimizing effort
estimates, producing more reliable and accurate forecasts.

**5.5 Values of A and B parameters of COCOMO-II**

The COCOMO-II model’s coefficients A and B are essential
in estimating the effort required for software development.
To address parameter sensitivity, we have tested a range
of values for the key parameters A(values [2,5]), B(values

[0.5,1.5]), and selected the combinations that produced the
best performance. This tuning process helped ensure the
model’s stability and effectiveness without relying on fixed
or arbitrary parameter settings. The Table 10 presents a
summary of different algorithms that were used to optimize
these coefficients for the NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81,
China, Desharnais, and Maxwell datasets.

projects.

In Table 10, we can see the optimized COCOMO-II
coefficients (A and B) across various algorithms applied to
enhance effort estimation for a specific dataset. The baseline
model uses standard values (A = 2.94, B = 0.91), which are
adjusted by each algorithm to better fit the data. For exam-­
ple, the Bat algorithm sets (A = 2.34, B = 1.18), reflecting
its echolocation-driven exploration. GA applies evolution-­
ary optimization, resulting in (A = 4.14, B = 0.85). Dolphinbased models set higher B values, with the Dolphin Bat
hybrid refining them to (A = 3.28, B = 1.10). The CFAEE
and FA models achieve balanced tuning, with CFAEE opti-­
mizing to (A = 3, B = 1.01), supporting more adaptive and
accurate estimations.

In the COCOMO81 dataset, the standard COCOMO-II
uses (A = 2.94, B = 0.91), but Bat adjusts this to (A = 2.00, B
= 0.96), implying a stronger scaling with size. GA increases
B significantly to (A = 2.50, B = 0.93), while the Dolphin
and Dolphin Bat models also raise both parameters. FA
decreases A and increases b with (A = 2.53, B = 1.03), and
CFAEE finds a balance with (A = 3, B = 0.97), improving
generalization across COCOMO81’s diverse project types.

For the China dataset, the Bat algorithm outputs (A =
2.50, B = 1.09), while CSHS rises to (A = 3.31, B = 1.05).
Dolphin models again show higher B values, reflecting
increased non-linearity. The FA model stays consistent with
(A = 3.01, B = 1.03). CFAEE applies enhanced exploration
and sets (A = 3.03, B = 1.01), achieving adaptive tuning

suitable for the dataset’s functional-size-based estimation
structure. Table 10 lists the A and B coefficients for the
Desharnais dataset. CSHS and Dolphin algorithms raise the
values of both coefficients (A=3.50, B=1.21), which shows
increased baseline effort scaling. GA (A = 3.12, B = 1.29)
and Bat (A = 3.28, B = 1.23) optimization yields, showing a
high sensitivity to project scale. Both FA and CFAEE mod-­

= 1.01), with CFAEE enhancing robustness through adap-­
tive coefficient tuning.

For the Maxwell dataset, the CSHS algorithm optimizes
the coefficients to A=3.23 and B=1.06, which shows the
nonlinearity. Bat, GA, and dolphin algorithms increase
effort predictions highly, which shows that these models
are highly sensitive to this dataset. The FA model remains
stable at (A = 3.14, B = 0.98). CFAEE, through chaos-driven
parameter tuning, produces (A = 3.01, B = 0.98), maintain-­
ing an equilibrium between underestimation and overestima-­
tion. The differences in A and B coefficients for the datasets
NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, and
Maxwell reveal that the various models symbolize the nonlinearity in the effort estimation, and the different values are
scaled by each model, as shown in Table 10. These accurate
and consistent effort assessments across various projects are
likely due to the balanced adjustments made by the CFAEE
model’s coefficients.

**5.6 Results of MMRE and PRED**

To answer RQ2, we have analyzed the results of MMRE
(Mean Magnitude of Relative Error) and PRED (0.25) met-­
rics to compare our proposed model, CFAEE, with other
models like COCOMO-II, GA, CSHS, Bat, Dolphin, Dol-­
phin Bat, and FA. This comparison shows that CFAEE gives
more accuracy than other models concerning MMRE and
PRED for the datasets NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81,
China, Desharnais, and Maxwell.

Table 11 shows a comprehensive comparison of
the Mean Magnitude of Relative Error (MMRE) val-­
ues across six benchmark datasets NASA93, NASA60,
COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, and Maxwell for the
baseline COCOMO-II model and its variants enhanced by

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

**Fig. 2** MMRE for different datasets

optimization algorithms: CSHS, GA, Bat, Dolphin, Dolphin
Bat, Firefly Algorithm (FA), and the proposed CFAEE. In
general, the default COCOMO-II model shows the high-­
est MMREs across all datasets, such as 81.582 (Maxwell),
74.389 (China), and 57.400 (NASA93), demonstrating its
limitations without parameter tuning. CSHS and GA provide
moderate improvements, reducing MMREs in some datas-­
ets like Desharnais (30.236 and 29.946, respectively) and
NASA93. The Bat, Dolphin, and Dolphin Bat algorithms
further reduce MMREs, particularly in NASA60 and China.
FA consistently delivers better performance than earlier
models across datasets, such as 26.791 (COCOMO81) and
10.500 (NASA60). Among all models, CFAEE consistently
achieves the lowest MMRE values in every dataset, includ-­
ing 8.662 (NASA60), 20.858 (COCOMO81), and 33.191
(Desharnais), confirming its superior adaptability and


accuracy across both large-scale and medium-scale projects.
The proposed CFAEE model consistently achieved the best
estimation accuracy across all datasets, and its results are
highlighted in bold in the Table 11.

We used the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank (WSR) test to assess
whether the improvements of our proposed model over oth-­
ers are statistically significant. When evaluating statisti-­
cal hypotheses to determine the significance of the results,
the p-value is necessary. Statistical significance is usually
defined as a p-value of less than 0.05, indicating strong evi-­
dence against the null hypothesis. In order to get over these
limitations, researchers also provide the effect size, which
quantifies the magnitude of the effect. We also used Cohen’s
d effect size to measure the practical significance of differ-­
ences, where values around 0.2 indicate small, 0.5 medium,

The statistical significance of CFAEE’s improvements
over other models is confirmed using the Wilcoxon SignedRank Test. All p-values comparing CFAEE to the other
## 1 3

models are below 0.05, indicating that its performance gains
are statistically significant across all datasets. The p-value is
smallest when compared with CSHS (0.0025), followed by
GA (0.0070), further validating the effectiveness of CFAEE
against strong baselines. In terms of practical impact, the
effect size analysis shows large improvements: 1.1786 for
CSHS, 1.1427 for GA, and 0.9510 for Bat, indicating that
CFAEE’s improvements are not only statistically significant
but also meaningful in practice. Dolphin and Dolphin Bat
show moderate effect sizes (0.7422 and 0.7090), confirm-­
ing CFAEE’s advantage. Although FA performs closely to
CFAEE, the effect size is 0.1242, suggesting that CFAEE
still maintains a consistent edge. Overall, these results dem-­
onstrate that CFAEE delivers the most accurate, statistically
significant, and practically relevant effort estimations across
diverse datasets and optimization scenarios.

International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management

Table 12 illustrates the PRED values for six benchmark
datasets, NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81, China, Deshar-­
nais, and Maxwell, for different algorithms. In PRED,
higher values indicate better estimation performance. The
default COCOMO-II model consistently yields the low-­
est PRED values across all datasets, such as 5.235 (Max-­
well), 6.660 (NASA60), and 7.526 (NASA93), indicating
poor prediction accuracy. Metaheuristic models like GA
and CSHS show moderate improvements, particularly in
datasets like China (31.000 and 29.990) and Desharnais
(22.022 and 33.303). The Dolphin, Dolphin Bat, and Bat
models further improve PRED scores across NASA93,
NASA60, and China. FA significantly boosts predictive
accuracy with PRED values such as 40.000 (NASA93)
and 57.142 (COCOMO81). Notably, the proposed CFAEE
model achieves the highest PRED scores across all datasets,
including 85.714 (NASA60), 71.428 (COCOMO81), and
50.000 (NASA93), confirming its superior performance.

To statistically validate these improvements, the Wil-­
coxon Signed-Rank (WSR) test was done, and results are
shown in the Table 12. This confirms that the observed
improvements in PRED are statistically significant across all
models. The lowest p-value is observed for GA (0.0274) and
CSHS (0.0314), reinforcing CFAEE’s consistent advantage.
Additionally, Cohen’s d effect size was used to assess the
magnitude of improvements. Large effect sizes are observed
for comparisons with GA (1.2489), CSHS (1.2396), and Bat
(1.0041), indicating a strong practical impact. Dolphin and
Dolphin Bat also show large effects (1.0616 and 0.9793),
while FA shows a moderate effect size (0.4041), suggest-­
ing that although FA is competitive, CFAEE still offers
substantial improvements. These results affirm that CFAEE
provides not only statistically reliable but also practically
meaningful enhancements in predictive performance across
diverse software estimation datasets.

The MMRE and PRED performance of several models,
including COCOMO-II, GA, Bat, Dolphin, Dolphin Bat,
FA, and CFAEE, for the NASA93, NASA60, COCOMO81,
China, Desharnais, and Maxwell datasets are shown in Fig-­
ures 2 and 3 respectively. It is observed that MMRE and
PRED values across all datasets demonstrate the superior-­
ity of the proposed CFAEE model. It consistently yields the
lowest MMRE values, indicating minimal prediction error,
and achieves the highest PRED values, reflecting a greater
proportion of accurate predictions within acceptable thresh-­
olds. This visual representation reinforces CFAEE’s robust-­
ness and reliability in delivering accurate and consistent
software effort estimations when compared to other com-­
peting models.

Table 13 presents the average execution time of each
model, highlighting the trade-off between accuracy and
computational cost. While CFAEE takes the longest time


(120 s), its superior performance justifies the additional
computation compared to simpler models like COCOMOII. The increased execution time of CFAEE is primarily due
to its enhanced exploration mechanisms and chaotic opti-­
mization strategy. It remains computationally feasible for
real-world applications and offers significant improvements
in prediction accuracy.

**6 Threats to validity**

This section discusses the possible risks to the validity of
our study’s experimental results.

**6.1 Internal validity**

Chaotic maps enhance search space exploration, helping the
algorithm avoid local optima and improve accuracy. Inte-­
grating CFAEE with COCOMO-II supports better param-­
eter calibration for more precise effort estimates. To reduce
bias from parameter settings, we tested a range of values
for A and B and chose the optimized value having the best
performance. CFAEE can adapt to different datasets through
fine-tuning and improving estimation accuracy. However,
incorrect setup for COCOMO-II parameters such as effort
multipliers and scale factors, may lead to biased or inac-­
curate estimates. To mitigate this, we followed the effort
multiplier ratings used in the existing study (Boehm 1984).

**6.2 External validity**

In this investigation, we meticulously analyzed multiple
projects of different sizes from the NASA and PROMISE
repositories. Our model’s applicability may be assessed
through further validation with some open-source or com-­
mercial projects. We have provided a comprehensive expla-­
nation of the proposed methodology with step-by-step
algorithm. This allows replicated studies with different proj-­
ects to validate our findings, thereby enhancing the external
validity of our study.

**6.3 Construct validity**

Our study employed two widely accepted evaluation met-­
rics: the mean magnitude of relative error (MMRE) and the
prediction at 25% (PRED). These metrics, commonly used
in many studies, measure the accuracy of effort estimation
and the percentage of projects for which the estimated effort
is within a given range of the actual effort. By using these
established measures, we have minimized the potential for
any threats to the validity of our experimental results.
## 1 3

**6.4 Conclusion validity**

Using the Chaotic Firefly Algorithm with Enhanced Explora-­
tion (CFAEE) in conjunction with the COCOMO-II model,
we carefully examined the data to guarantee the validity of
the study’s conclusions. The careful selection of evalua-­
tion metrics, such as the mean magnitude of relative error
(MMRE) and the prediction at the 25% level (PRED), allows
us to confidently conclude the effectiveness of our proposed
approach over different models. We also ran the experiment
several times, validating our results by contrasting them with
existing models. Therefore, the impact of this threat on the
outcome of our experimental findings is minimal.

**7 Conclusion and future work**

Software development Estimation is a vital stage in the
software development life cycle (SDLC). Accurate soft-­
ware development estimation ensures a smooth progres-­
sion towards project completion. In this paper, we have
used the Firefly algorithm (FA) and Chaotic Firefly Algo-­
rithm with Enhanced Exploration (CFAEE) to optimize
the COCOMO-II model’s parameters (A and B). We have
evaluated the performance of different models such as
COCOMO-II, Genetic Algorithm, Cuckoo Optimization
and Harmony Search algorithm, Bat, Dolphin, Dolphin Bat,
FA, and CFAEE, using projects from NASA93, NASA60,
COCOMO81, China, Desharnais, and Maxwell datasets.
Our proposed CFAEE method outperformed the other mod-­
els by examining the MMRE and PRED results. The CFAEE
model acquired lower estimation errors and improved the
predictive accuracy for all datasets. In order to demonstrate
the superiority of the proposed model over certain current
models, we conducted a statistical wilcoxon signed-rank
analysis of the data. These results show the possibility of
CFAEE being a sophisticated effort estimation method that
can give more accurate predictions and be more dependable
than conventional models and various metaheuristic-based

models. Future research can be extended by incorporating a
broader range of projects from multiple datasets to validate
the generalizability of the proposed approach across diverse
software development scenarios. Additionally, ensembling
the proposed approach with other effort estimation models
such as Case-Based Reasoning and Machine Learning tech-­
niques, may further enhance predictive accuracy.
